subtopic: LEBANON

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LEBANON
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO STEPS TAKEN BY UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to give a statement to the house. I desire to inform the house of the steps which the United Nations is taking in connection with the crisis in Lebanon, and the role which Canada is once again being called upon to play.
The security council resolution of June 11 under which the United Nations group in Lebanon is functioning grew out of the complaint submitted by Lebanon regarding interference in its affairs by the United Arab Republic. The operative part of the resolution-passed, as hon. members of the house I am sure know, with the full concurrence of 10 of the 11* members of the council, including Canada, with only the U.S.S.R. abstaining-meets the essential requirements of a constructive United Nations intervention. It calls for the urgent dispatch of an observation group to proceed to Lebanon-and I quote from the resolution that was adopted by the security council:
... so as to ensure that there is no illegal infiltration of personnel or supply of arms or other materiel across the Lebanese border;
-and it authorizes the secretary general to take the necessary steps to that end.
Because of the need for haste the secretary general turned in the first instance to the United Nations truce supervision organization in Palestine-UNTSO-to form the nucleus of the substantial military observer corps that he will require to assist the political team of three which will constitute the observation group proper. This team consists of three highly qualified and experienced men selected

Lebanon-United Nations Intervention by the secretary general; a Norwegian, an Ecuadorian, and an Indian. The Norwegian -General Bull, commander of the Norwegian air force-arrived in Beirut on June 15, preceded a day or two earlier by 15 military observers from the UNTSO staff, including one Canadian, Major G. D. Mitchell. All these UNTSO officers are assigned on a temporary basis only, but I need hardly say that the secondment of a Canadian officer from the TSO to this urgent and highly important task of getting the UN operation under way was arranged with the full approval of our Department of National Defence.
General Bull had not been on the ground for more than a few hours when it became apparent to him that the modest sized observer corps which had at first been envisaged would be entirely inadequate for the task in hand, having regard to the complexity of the situation and the mountainous nature of the frontier areas. He promptly reported to the secretary general that a minimum of 100 military observers would be essential to the success of the operation. The secretary general thereupon requested Canada and 13 other countries to supply additional observers from their regular armed forces on a basis of the utmost urgency. Of the other countries so approached Finland, Netherlands, Norway, Italy, Chile and Denmark have accepted, and several others are momentarily expected to do so.
I need hardly tell the house that the Canadian government too has responded speedily to the secretary general's appeal. Ten Canadian officers have already been chosen for this assignment, and they should be on their way to Lebanon within 48 hours. The ultimate scope of the United Nations operations in Lebanon is not yet clear, and the secretary general himself is leaving for Beirut tonight to examine the situation on the spot.
The task with which he and the observation group have been entrusted by the security council is a delicate and difficult one. The success or failure of this initiative has, of course, immediate significance for Lebanon's security and possibly for peace in the area as a whole. But it could have far wider implications; it represents a further test, perhaps a crucial one, of the United Nations ability to deal rapidly and effectively with international disputes of a kind likely to lead to open conflict.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. D.	S. Harkness	(Minister	of
Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Essex East asked this question, as found at page 1159 of Hansard:
I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if 'his attention has been directed to a statement made to the soybean growers by the chairman of the agricultural prices stabilization board as to the way in which the floor price for soybeans is intended to operate? If the minister has not seen that statement, would he be prepared to look at It and advise the house as to whether or not that is a correct statement of the application of this floor price policy?
The so-called statement actually is a letter which was written by the chairman of the board to Mr. Standing of the Ontario soybean growers marketing board, and the letter conveys correctly our ideas, on the basis of information we have received so far from the soybean growers marketing board, as to how support will have to operate. In order that other hon. members may know what we are talking about perhaps I should read a few paragraphs from the letter which outlines the situation. The letter states in part:
I believe you understand that this stabilization assistance is to be in the form of a deficiency payment whereby this board will make up the difference between the average return to all growers and the prescribed price.
We believe your board-
That is the soybean marketing board.
-regulates the price of all the product for the growers and it is understood that you will be keeping a record of each producer's deliveries and the return per bushel which he receives ... we will need to be able to determine the average sale price per bushel for all grades and then the difference between this average price received by all growers and the stabilization price of $2.10 per bushel will be paid to each eligible grower.
This is the way it will operate. We will say that the average price that is received for soybeans is $2 a bushel. That will mean there will be a deficiency payment of 10 cents per bushel which we will make up. But the beans from each individual grower will have been sold at different prices by their own board. Some of that difference will be due to the time at which they are sold. Some farmers will perhaps be holding their beans for four months before they are sold; others will sell them practically out of the field. Second, the difference would be due to variations in grade.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In any event, the only thing we can do is make up the average difference. Whatever that sum is-we will say it is 10 cents in this case-it will be paid to each grower which will mean, of course, that each grower will not receive the same price for his beans. The only way in which they can receive the same price for their beans is if the soybean growers marketing board and the growers themselves are willing to pool their returns, as is done by the wheat growers of western Canada under the Canadian wheat board. If they are willing to pool their returns there is, of course, no difficulty in connection with the matter. These people can then receive the same return. If they are not willing to pool their returns, which is their own decision, there is no way in which the returns can be made exactly the same to each of them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 4, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith (Perth)-Mr. Sevi-gny in the chair:
That It Is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to authorize contributions being made as

of the first day of July, 1958, to a participating province which has a plan in operation; and to make certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a week ago, at about two minutes before six o'clock, I began to make some comments on this subject. Today I should like to continue my remarks with regard to the proposed amendments to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
I said at that time that I was aware from my own experience of the need for some type of hospital insurance; that I had attended the last dominion-provincial conference on this subject, and had been impressed by the fact that most of the spokesmen for the provinces had expressed the need for hospital insurance in their particular provinces. They had also expressed the need for federal aid.
The cost per patient day has been going up steadily all across Canada. In Ontario, for example, the cost in 1941 was $3.47, while in 1956 it was $14.46; and in no intervening year has there been a decrease in these costs.
I have here a copy of the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of May 30 from which I will read a few extracts. It cost nearly half a billion dollars to run the hospitals of Canada in 1956. The total expenditures for hospitals of all types rose by more than 11 per cent to the record figure of $467,500,000, representing an average per capita cost of about $29. Public hospitals, including federal, private, mental and tubercular hospitals, reported expenditures of $347 million. It cost $3,583 to maintain the average public hospital bed in operation for the year, as against $3,379 a year before. The average cost per patient day in 1956 was $13 as compared with $12.26 in 1955, while in 1952 the daily cost was $2.47.
Costs have varied according to the size and nature of the hospital concerned. The figures 'give the breakdown of costs under salaries and wages, drugs and medical supplies, food and so on. One thing struck me particularly, the fact that in Canada we are giving less voluntary help to our hospitals. According to the dominion bureau of statistics this decreasing dependence on voluntary public support is illustrated by the fact that donations from the public for current operations provide only $16.10 of every $1,000 of general hospital revenue, as compared with $17.43 two years previously.
The highest figure for public donations was $30.32 per $1,000 of revenue in Quebec, and the lowest was $1.50 in Alberta.
With this background of rising hospital costs in mind, and taking into consideration

the mental stress and financial worries attendant upon prolonged illnesses, our former prime minister decided to make available to the provinces the best available hospital and diagnostic care. The federal government would assume approximately half the cost while the provinces would assume the other half, the only stipulation being that these services should be available to every person resident within a province. In my opinion that was one of the greatest humanitarian acts ever placed on the statute books of Canada. This act was piloted through the House of Commons by the former minister of national health and welfare, now the hon. member for Essex East, who received a well deserved and merited compliment the other day from the hon. member for Durham when he referred to the great part played by the hon. member for Essex East in putting this legislation on our statute books.
Provision was made that this act should come into operation as soon as six provinces had signed the agreement and could qualify under the act. I can well remember the criticisms that were voiced in this house. I well remember the statements made by the former hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Knowles, who maintained that this act should go into operation immediately and should apply to those provinces that had hospital plans already in force. I well remember certain hon. members now to your right maintaining at that time that this act should apply to depreciation and administrative costs, and that it should provide for payment of half the costs for mental and tubercular patients in those institutions.
I well remember the fine argument put forward by my friend the late hon. member for Lanark, Dr. Blair. He insisted that there should be no differentiation between sickness in a general hospital and sickness in a mental or tuberculosis hospital. In fact hon. members on the other side of the house, and particularly the present Minister of Finance, criticized the exclusions contained in section 2 (e) of the bill. The Minister of Finance, the then private hon. member for Eglinton, felt so keenly about it that he divided the house on third reading of the bill. As I recall it the present Minister of National Health and Welfare and many hon. members who now sit on your right voted with him.
I refer to page 3381 of Hansard of April 10, 1957, where an amendment moved by the present Minister of Finance is recorded in these words:
That Bill 320 be not now read the third time, but that the said bill be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering the provisions to exclude tuberculosis hospitals
Hospital Insurance Act and sanatoria and hospitals and institutions for the mentally ill in clause 2 (e) thereof.
He went on to state:
My purpose is to ask the house to refer the bill back to the committee of the whole in order that this same clause which contains this unjustifiably narrow definition of the word "hospital" may be reconsidered. I put before the house the ground that there can be no justification in good sense or in principle or in humanity or in the existing facts of life as applied to the financial difficulties of the provinces and municipalities of this country, for this government to try to drive a wedge between general hospitals on the one hand and tuberculosis hospitals and sanatoria and hospitals and institutions for the mentally ill on the other hand. It is only by changing the definition that the government proposes in clause 2 (e) that this unworthy distinction can be eliminated.
The hon. member at that time argued that there could be no justification whatever for the exclusion of those hospitals. I wish to refer briefly to the remarks made by the present Prime Minister with regard to this amendment proposed by the present Minister of Finance. On April 10, 1957, as recorded at page 3386 of Hansard, the Prime Minister, the then private hon. member for Prince Albert, said:
The amendment moved by the hon. member would refer the bill to the committee of the whole for the purpose of considering this clause and thereby giving an opportunity, even at this late hour, of including within the ambit of the legislation sanatoria, tuberculosis hospitals and institutions and hospitals for the mentally ill. I cannot understand this omission.
It is interesting to note that the right hon. gentleman who now sits in this house as Prime Minister pursued this matter in the election campaign that year. The Winnipeg Tribune of May 14, 1957, reports him as having said:
The Conservatives, he said, would repair a "serious omission" in the federal health plan which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
The Toronto Globe and Mail of May 28, 1957, reports the hon. gentleman as having said in Saskatoon:
Mr. Diefenbaker said the Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions.
I consider that in these statements, if correct-and I have no reason to accuse either the Globe and Mail or the Winnipeg Tribune of not being correct-we have a solemn promise to the people of Canada. I am certainly surprised in view of this fact that section 2 (e) is not being amended by the government at this time to widen the definition in order to cover mental and tuberculosis hospitals.
I was interested in seeing what some of the provinces thought about the bill. The

Hospital Insurance Act Vancouver Province of March 8, 1958, carried the following report:
Premier Bennett made his first direct criticism of the national Conservative government.
"We are a little alarmed." he told the house "at the way the present government is holding hands with Ontario and Quebec; it is a little too much for the best interests of British Columbia."
Earlier he said:
I am terribly disappointed in the Diefenbaker government. I had hoped that it would have had vision. Actually it has dealt with British Columbia more severely than the Liberal government did.
In the 10 months since this government was elected it has been in the business of politics rather than that of government. To digress a little, I certainly believe that, because in my own riding unemployment is increasing in spite of the promises that we would have no unemployment by the middle of the summer.

The minister of health of British Columbia said this:
The Tories have stated mental care and tuberculosis care can't be accepted as shareable hospital insurance costs without impairment of payments made provinces under other arrangements.
The best compliment this government is paying to the former government is contained in the proposed amendments to this act. One has to do with getting the scheme started; otherwise the scheme could not get started. The other minor amendment has to do with providing some meals and restricting the use


of drugs. I would like the minister to tell us what Premier Bennett has in mind. I would like to know whether British Columbia was offered a deal different from that signed by Ontario. I know the minister said the other day that Newfoundland had signed an agreement. I would like him to tell us whether there was any difference in detail in the agreement signed by Ontario and the agreement signed by the province of Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They are all within the terms of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am asking whether there was any difference in detail. I would like to know why the other provinces have not signed. It seems to me that there must be some difference or British Columbia would have signed. It looks to me as though this government got the province of Ontario to sign and is offering this amendment as bait to the other provinces to come in so as not to embarrass the province of Ontario on January 1, 1959, if six provinces have not come into the scheme by that time. I really think this government is forced to bring in this amendment as the result of its own failure to pursue the parliamentary objective of having a nation-wide hospital insurance plan under way as soon as possible.
I think the act itself is excellent; I believe the formula worked out by the previous government was an ingenious one. It tends to prevent any interference on the part of the Department of National Health and Welfare in things that come purely within provincial jurisdiction. The act itself is generous and it will readily be taken up by the people. I think, however, this scheme would have been very difficult of attainment without the national health program that we had in force under the former minister for a period of 10 years or more. We spent something like $250 million under that program. We helped to provide beds in new hospitals and hospital extensions. We spent much money in the control of such diseases as tuberculosis, venereal disease and cancer. We also spent much money in training large numbers of personnel.
One very good example of the action taken by the former minister was the help given to the provinces to get their poliomyelitis immunization programs under way. As a result the incidence of polio has dropped. I have not seen the recent figures, but I know it has come down very markedly. The dominion government spent $3 million on that program. There has been a great saving to the people, not only in hospital beds because those people are not in the hospitals for prolonged periods, but because many children are not going to be handicapped for life.

One outstanding feature of the bill, of course, is the fact that there is no time limit on hospitalization. I know from personal experience that many people who suffer multiple fractures and terminal illnesses are often in hospital much longer than they could be and still be covered by the insurance schemes at present in vogue. Hospitals also should be able to budget and not have large deficits. The municipalities should benefit when this scheme is in operation. If the provinces play fair with the municipalities, the municipalities will not have to put up their share for indigent people going to hospital. We have old age pensioners, old age assistance cases and various other civil pensioners who go to hospitals; and if the provinces assume their share then the municipalities will be relieved financially.
Dr. Malcolm G. Taylor of the University of Toronto was commissioned by the Canadian tax foundation to submit his findings concerning the probable cost of hospital and medical care in Canada, and by a series of calculations he came up with a figure showing that our national hospital insurance scheme would cost something like $634 million by 1960. Dr. Taylor thinks we should be able to do this and I certainly think we should, since this figure is just a little over half our liquor bill in Canada.

speechtext: That is for 10 provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, 10 provinces. He estimated that by 1960 the combined cost in Canada of medical and hospital care would be 2.6 per cent of our national income, whereas today it is 2 per cent.
One thing I like about this scheme is the fact that people will be able to go to hospital as of right and not be classified as indigents. We have a highly educated public. They are all aware of the benefits of good health care, and they look upon the rising standards of medical care as concomitants of a rising standard of living. Therefore, but for the hospital scheme we have put on the statute books, I think we would have had increased hospital and medical care.
I know the minister is very anxious to answer some of these questions. I have tabulated certain questions which I should like to hear him answer before we adopt the resolution. First I should like him to tell us why more provinces have not signed agreements. There have only been two and there certainly should have been six by this time. I think we would have had six if the minister had pursued the matter more vigorously. Second, what is the reason for British Columbia's attitude? I have heard from other sources that British Columbia does
Hospital Insurance Act not look on the plan very favourably. Third, were all provinces offered the same agreement? In spite of what the minister said in the house the other day I have heard that there is some difference between the agreements signed by Ontario and Newfoundland.	.
I have one last question, and I am sure the minister can answer it very easily. Why do the minister, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the minister's other colleagues take such a restricted view of section 2 (e) of the act, when they all voted to include hospitalization in mental and tubercular institutions on April 10, 1957?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have just heard some very interesting remarks from the hon. member for Welland who speaks, I understand, as a medical practitioner. His views on this subject are most interesting. I will have to speak as a patient of various medical practitioners throughout the country and try to give the viewpoint of the patient with regard to this matter.
I believe there are many phases of the hospital insurance plan that are badly in need of explanation at the present time. I quite realize that some of the problems I may raise are not caused wholly by the federal government, but I believe the federal government has a duty and responsibility to the people, particularly of the province of Ontario, to try to correct some of the wrong impressions that have been created in the minds of the people and to clear up some of the confusion and misinformation under which the people of Ontario are labouring at the present time.
The first point I should like to refer to, and in my opinion it is a serious fault in the plan, has to do with the fact that there is no coverage for old age pensioners. Throughout the country there are examples of hospital insurance plans that have been in effect for quite a number of years and have worked very satisfactorily, and which do not lack such a provision. This is not a new field we are plowing. Examples, figures, information and data are all available. I think such a provision definitely should be included in this plan; and as long as amendments are being made to the scheme we should certainly include the major amendments needed to make the plan as good as it possibly can be made.
There is another aspect with regard to old age pensions which I believe will cause a lot of confusion. As I understand the situation, people who are drawing old age assistance will be covered by the plan made effective by the agreement between the
1212	HOUSE OF
Hospital Insurance Act province of Ontario and the federal government so far as their hospital costs are concerned. However, when they pass from the 65 to 70 old age assistance group, during which time they receive a pension with a means test, to the group 70 and over who automatically receive an old age pension with no means test, I understand they will have to obtain a certificate proving they are indigent or in very needy circumstances or they will automatically lose their hospital plan benefits. I think that is a point that needs very close scrutiny. If the situation is as it appears to be from the information I have received so far, it is certainly something that should be corrected.
The information I have referred to is contained in the literature being published concerning the plan at the present time. On page 8 of the booklet I have here which has to do with questions and answers about hospital insurance in Ontario there is a reference to social assistance persons. There is a further reference to page 50, where one finds a description of the various people who will be eligible. One sees that persons who qualify under the Old Age Assistance Act are eligible, and then it says that persons who come under the Old Age Security Act and are approved by the department of public welfare are eligible to receive medical welfare services.
Because of that information and subsequent telephone calls and inquiries I have made I have gained the impression that a person receiving old age assistance, with respect to whom the means test is automatically abolished at age 70, will have to apply for a certificate of financial distress, shall we say, or he will automatically lose his hospital benefits under the plan.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Can my hon. friend be more precise? That is a very important statement to make. Perhaps the minister might comment on it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE CONTRIBUTIONS TO PARTICIPATING PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
,1 am hoping that the minister will comment and clarify the point if he has the information available because, as I understand the situation from the information I have obtained, the only way old age pensioners, those 70 and over, can obtain these benefits is by obtaining a certificate to the effect that they are in needy circumstances. This would mean that they would automatically lose the benefits they have had from age 65 to 70 unless they were fully aware of the situation and obtained the necessary certificate.
There is another matter which I think should be given very close scrutiny and consideration at this time. Under the plan as it has been outlined there is no assurance as there is, for example, under the Ontario Blue


Cross plan, that the current monthly rates will remain the same even for the period of one year, as they now do under Blue Cross. Under the Blue Cross plan, the most common hospital plan in Ontario at the present time, you at least have a guarantee for one year as to what the plan is going to cost you. There is no guarantee under the proposed plan, I understand, and that is borne out by a question asked at a meeting held in January, 1958. In Industrial Canada for February, 1958, I find the following question:
Will the commission be able to guarantee the premiums set by it lor any specific period, as does the Blue Cross?
This was the answer:
No. It is hoped that the rates will hold but if hospital costs rise payments to hospitals will have to rise.
It would seem, Mr. Chairman, that clarification of this very important matter is required. Under this set-up, insured persons would seem to have no guarantee against sudden fluctuations in insurance costs.
Another very important matter is that there is no provision at the present time in any way, shape or form for the waiving of premiums of people who are unfortunate enough to have a prolonged stay in the hospital. There is no obligation of any kind on companies or employers to provide coverage for those people, and certainly common sense tells us that after an extended stay in the hospital a man is far from able to pick up and continue his hospitalization premiums. I feel this matter should be given very careful consideration, and certainly some action taken in that respect.
The hon. member who spoke before me made some mention of the case of indigents. From what I have gathered about this particular plan I believe indigents are divided into two categories. The first category is that of patients who are permanently in the indigent class. They, of course, are provided for under the present plan. I believe a considerable amount of confusion and possible distress could be caused amongst patients in the other category, that is people who, through no fault of their own, may be temporarily placed in the indigent patient class. This could result from unemployment or some other factor of that kind.
Possibly a little later I should like to deal with the particular cost aspects of this matter. Actually the arrangements that have been worked out, as we understand them and in spite of the very clear stand taken by many members of the present cabinet just one year ago, still fail to include the cost of mental and tubercular cases. I should like to quote just one paragraph from Hansard

for April 10, 1957, page 3380. These are the words of the present Minister of Finance, who said:
We as a party and as Her Majesty's loyal opposition have already expressed in the strongest terms our view that there is no justification whatever for the exclusion of these hospitals and institutions from among those that lie within the scope of the scheme of hospital insurance.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think the minister owes all of us in this house an explanation as to why there is such a change from that very definite stand of just one year ago.
There is another matter upon which I should like to have some clarification from the minister, if he is in a position to do so. Over the last few months there has been a considerable amount of newspaper advertising concerning the new Ontario hospital plan which will be established the first of next year. These advertisements usually contain an address to which one can write if one needs further information. I had a case drawn to my attention in which a person wrote to this address requesting further information about the new hospital plan, and to my amazement the reply had nothing whatever to do with the hospital plan but was a very colourful advertisement for the Ontario Blue Cross plan for supplementary benefits that could be purchased over and above the regular hospital plan. This raises a question in my mind, sir, as to whether the costs of this advertising for another plan are included in the costs of the Ontario hospitalization plan which, in the opinion of many thinking people, appear to be rather high.
This brings me to my next point, which is the cost of this plan. Most of us realize that the plan presently proposed is on the basis of $2.10 per month for a single person and $4.20 per month for a family. People generally have been given the idea that that is only one third of the cost and the other two thirds are borne equally by the provincial and federal governments. In fact I have here a copy of a pamphlet entitled "Facts about Hospital Care Insurance; for Residents of Ontario". On page 4 I read:
The projected total cost of the hospital insurance program for 1959, including care and treatment in mental and tuberculosis hospitals, is about $210 million.
Revenue from premiums will total about $75 million, or about one-third of the cost of the total program. The balance is being financed by general revenues of the federal and provincial governments. Each level of government will bear approximately one-third of the cost.
I should like to point out that those figures are certainly very misleading. As I understand this plan, and this is subject to correction-I would be glad if the minister
Hospital Insurance Act would inform me if I am wrong-the arrangement is that the federal government will pay one half the cost of hospital patients in Ontario, excluding tuberculosis and mental patients. I have also received information that tuberculosis and mental patients take up roughly one half the hospital beds in this country. This would mean that the federal contribution would not be one third but merely one half of one half, which according to my arithmetic means one quarter. The premiums of individual groups supporting this plan will amount to roughly $75 million as estimated in this pamphlet, which is in fact 36 per cent of the estimated $210 million. Well, with the federal government paying 25 per cent and the individual 36 per cent, this leaves 39 per cent for the Ontario government. If we translate that into dollars it means the federal government would pay $52.5 million, the individual premium payer $75 million, and the Ontario government $82.5 million. This is definitely not the picture presented by the various data put out by the province of Ontario.
There is another interesting point, and that is the additional coverage which may be purchased through the various private companies. The information we have received is that a person will be able to pay through the Ontario commission not only the premiums covering the Ontario hospital plan but also any additional premiums for private coverage by a private company. In other words the commission is being used as a check-off for private insurance companies that may be selling additional coverage. Once again, sir, I wonder to whom these costs are charged, and whether or not we have been given a true picture of the actual costs of the hospitalization plan.
That brings me to the point I mentioned a little while ago, namely the arrangement with regard to temporary indigent patients. As I understand it, the situation at the present time is that these patients are going to be screened by the municipalities, and that once they are judged by the municipalities to be eligible for assistance, then the costs will be borne by the municipalities; but the costs coming back from the provincial government will not have any relation to the actual costs paid by the municipalities but rather will be on a per capita basis for the municipalities to use in any way they see fit.
In my opinion that procedure could lead to a situation where you could have your sidewalks paved and the cost charged to the hospital plan. In one sense possibly it does not make much difference, as far as
1214	HOUSE OF
Hospital Insurance Act the municipal taxpayer is concerned, which pocket it comes out of as long as he gets full value for his money. However, in all fairness to our hospitalization plan I think some better arrangement than this could be made. I would hope the minister would be able to answer some of these questions.

I shall try to answer a few of these questions that have been mentioned by hon. members.
The hon. member for Welland certainly presented some extremely interesting statistics with regard to rising costs generally, and he gave an amazing picture as to the cost jump from approximately $2 to $14 I think that was his last figure-in a comparatively short space of time. He mentioned the fact that we are not proposing any change in clause 2 (e) having to do with tuberculosis and mental hospitals. That is quite right. The situation has been unchanged since it was previously mentioned in this house, in fact since the last fiscal conference between the provinces and the federal government. He went to some pains to congratulate the hon. member for Essex East, and with those congratulations I agree wholeheartedly. However, I would point out that it took the previous government since 1919 to get around to bringing in hospital insurance. I should also like to point out that if they had still been in power no provincial governments would be participating; up to January 1, 1959, they would not be in receipt of federal funds.

The hon. member mentioned old age pensioners having to reapply when they become eligible for old age pensions at the age of 70 after having been on old age assistance. My understanding is that this is not so. It has been indicated to us that those who have been on old age assistance prior to age 70, when they reach the age of 70 and become subject to old age pension they will automatically come under the scheme and have their premiums paid.
As to the rates, here again this is purely a provincial matter as to how they raise their share of hospital costs. Some are going to do so by sales taxes, I presume. Some may do it out of general revenue. Others are doing it on a premium basis. The hon. member suggested that there is no guarantee that these rates may not be raised. That is quite so, but we understand no change is contemplated for some little time at least. Eventually there may have to be a change. I am not in a position to disagree with that possibility.
The hon. member for Skeena, speaking to this resolution earlier, suggested that we should give more consideration to prevention, which is important. I quite agree. In this respect I would point out that we are spending millions for research generally and for the prevention of disease. I feel that the hon. member for Skeena has made a very close study of this matter, and I should like to say that I greatly enjoyed the remarks he made in commenting on the hospitalization scheme.
I think I might give a brief resume of just what the situation is in the various provinces. There seems to have been some concern in the minds of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Welland to the effect that we had not gotten on with this scheme just as rapidly as we might. I should like to assure them that entirely the opposite has been the case. My officials have visited all the provinces. We have had many provincial officials visit Ottawa. We have had two technical conferences at the official level, with some ministers present. I have met with several ministers. Everything possible has been done to facilitate the signing of agreements with the provinces.
I should like to point out the situation, taking each province in turn. As the house has been informed and as hon. members know, Ontario has signed an agreement under date of March 3 last. This program will come into being on January 1, 1959. As to Newfoundland, the minister of health for Newfoundland and I signed an agreement on June 9.

It will come into effect on July 1, 1958 provided this legislation is passed in order to make it possible. As to Manitoba, the province has passed the requisite legislation. The agreement has been drawn up and is now ready for signing. This province plans to commence its program on July 1, 1958.

No, effective January 1, 1959. I have indicated that we expect five provinces to sign by July 1 so that their schemes can go into effect by that date. Nova Scotia is in the same position as New Brunswick, and it is expected that their programs will commence on January 1, 1959. I would like to quote from Hansard of 1956, at page 3228; the present Prime Minister, then the hon. member for Prince Albert, is reported as having said:
The transport controller has the power to order any person dealing with any bulk transport to transport goods in bulk, to fix minimum quotas, maximum ratios and so forth. So great are the powers conferred that, no matter what he does, as long as he acts within the powers conferred upon him there is no right of action. If any person fails to fulfil any contract or obligation because of the order of the controller, it is a good defence to an action against such a person to place before the court and prove the allegation that what was done was done pursuant to the order of the transport controller.
Then, later on, during the course of the same debate, at page 3274, the same gentleman had this to say:
So far as regulations are concerned I may say that the Supreme Court of Canada paid its tribute to the kind of regulations the minister's department has brought into being by referring to them as inconsistent with justice and derogatory of the rights of individuals.
Well, if that language, which was pretty strong at the time, still stands I would have believed that the minister would have thought it incumbent upon him not to demand the extension of those powers, without explanation. Then, again, in volume IV of Hansard of 1956, at page 3496, there is a quotation from the same gentleman that I would like to read:
The regulations provide for a transport controller having authority to order any person dealing in various bulk commodities to fix minimum quotas, to fix proportions and the like and also to order any person dealing in bulk transport facilities, which include railways, steamships and the like, to extend, furnish, supply or make use of any bulk transport facilities for transporting any bulk commodities.

These powers are very wide. The transport controller becomes almost, if not completely, omnipotent. His authority is above the law; his discretion is unchallengeable.
I would think that those qualifications of the powers of the transport controller, if he is appointed under the regulations as they are now before us, would be exactly the same today as they were then, because I presume there has been no amendment to those regulations and that is one of the questions which I would like to ask the minister. I hope he will be able to tell us whether, during the course of time his government has been in office, there has been any amendment to those regulations. I presume there have not been any but if there has been any I would hope they would be given to the house.
The government of Canada provided for the appointment of a transport controller in the month of August, 1951, under the Emergency Powers Act, and subsequently there was put in the statutes legislation generally known as Bill No. 443, and containing the terms of the order in council P.C. 4535. It was the opinion of the government at that time that due to the heavy demand upon all forms of transportation particularly lake and rail some authority was necessary to ensure an equitable distribution of the various bulk commodities such as grain, iron ore, coal, sand, pulpwood and the like. The main duties of the transport controller had to do with the hauling and handling of grain; first, to make sure that when grain is sold by the Canadian wheat board or any other exporter the grain moves freely to the seaboard port when the vessels present themselves for their loads; second, to see that transportation does not limit the amount of grain which can be sold by Canada.
There are, as the house knows, four outlets for the export of grain in this country. There is the Pacific coast outlet made up of the ports of Vancouver, New Westminster and Prince Rupert, all of which are open the year round. Then there is the port of Churchill which is open for a period of about two and a half months. There are also the St. Lawrence ports with a navigation season lasting for about eight months. Finally, there are the Atlantic ports of Halifax and Saint John which, while open for navigation all year, are used for the export of grain during the months of December to April inclusive when the St. Lawrence ports are closed.
At this moment I am particularly concerned with the movement of grain in the St. Lawrence area. I am sure that other members of the house will deal with the problems having to do with western Canada but as I speak at the moment I am particularly interested in the movement through St. Lawrence river
Department of Transport Act ports. This movement originates at the lake-head. The grain is moved in three circuits. First, grain is moved by means of lake carriers down the great lakes for trans-shipment at the ports of Port Colborne, Prescott or Kingston from where it is trans-shipped in canal-lers to Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec, Sorel and other such ports for further transshipment overseas. The second way is the lake and rail route. That shipment is by water to the bay ports and from the bay ports to Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports by rail. The third movement is an all water movement from the head of the lakes to Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports by means of canallers.
The reason I raise this matter is that there has been serious complaint at the port of Montreal that it has not been receiving a sufficient quantity of grain. In other words, the same quantity of grain that obtained in the past has not been there for transshipment overseas. I do not have the figures before me at the present time but I recall a recent statement made by the shipping authorities of the port of Montreal complaining bitterly that the movement of grain towards St. Lawrence ports was diminishing and was not nearly as substantial as it has been in the past. What are the reasons for this? I know they are manifold. I should like to bring the situation to the attention of the minister and say that one reason may well be the fact that a transport controller is not there to direct this movement of grain. That may have something to do with it.
I am sure there are other reasons. I am sure that the proximity of the Pacific coast ports to the wheat area also has a great deal to do with it and I am sure that rates have some influence on the situation. But I would direct the minister's attention particularly to the fact that there was no serious complaint in the past and I do not see why it is not possible to distribute the movement of grain in a more equitable manner. I realize that much of the grain moves during the short navigation season to the port of Churchill. There is an area within a certain radius of the port from which I presume it is much less costly to move grain to that port and from there to the United Kingdom market.
But the practice has grown up over the years to send a substantial movement to the port of Montreal and with the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and the fact that there are interests in the United States who state categorically that they will ship their wheat down this route to overseas markets by way of Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports it becomes more and more

Mr. Chairman, we in this
group have taken the position, since the war that a transport controller was needed for the efficient movement and allocation of box cars amongst elevator points on the prairies. However it seems to me the attitude taken by the government in presenting this resolution at this time is a very strange one. The Conservative party over the years objected to the former Liberal government being given wide, all-inclusive powers. The former minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, was castigated and criticized for having very wide powers which he could use at his discretion. It would seem to me that the Conservative party is not in a suitable role in presenting this motion, in the light of its traditions and in the light of its actions in this house for many years.
The Conservative party has always objected to wide powers being taken by the government under particular circumstances. We in this group have always been prepared to look at any given case on its merits. If we have felt that wide powers were necessary, we were quite prepared to grant them. I believe, and now I am talking from the standpoint of the Conservative party's record, that in presenting this resolution at this time they are on very weak ground. I say they are on weak ground because of the answer just given by the Minister of Transport. It is one thing to say we want wide powers when there is a specific job to do

that requires wide powers. It is another thing to say to this house, we want wide powers on a speculative basis to take care of some undisclosed, unstated emergency which might arise at some time in the future.
I should like to see the hon. member for Greenwood take a good look at this resolution, and try to judge for himself whether or not it is a wise thing for the government to ask for such broad powers for undisclosed and unstated purposes. There may be a need for such powers. As a matter of fact, I think there is a need for such powers. I do not feel I am being inconsistent. I should like to see a member of the government stand up and tell us what they are going to do with these powers, then let us judge the necessity for them on the basis of the proposed action. I do not think it is good enough for the minister to say, we want these powers and we may or may not use them. I ask the minister whether these powers might be connected with the Bracken commission inquiry into box car allocations. I see him shaking his head in the negative. I cannot conceive of anything else they might have to do with. I am quite prepared to stand corrected, but as the former minister of transport well knows and as the present minister knows, this act has been used exclusively or almost exclusively in connection with the movement of grain. I believe that little, if any, of the power has been used in connection with the other commodities named.
I cannot see why, therefore, the government should want these powers unless it contemplates using the powers. I cannot conceive of any use to which the powers might be put other than as a result of the report that Mr. John Bracken may be making at some future date. The government has told us of the very heavy agenda that faces parliament at this time. The speech from the throne indicated there might be a great deal of work for this session. We have asked the Prime Minister what action might be taken on Dr. Clark's report, which might lead to an increase in pensions paid to elderly people. His answer was that there was an abundance of work for this session. He did not feel for this reason that parliament should be asked to deal with any such report during this session. Yet we have a minister presenting a resolution at this time and saying he does not know to what use the powers might be put. He wants these powers for two years, but he does not know for what purpose. He just wants to have them around. This sounds worse than C. D. Howe used to sound when he wanted powers. speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Pori Arthur) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING COMPANIES IN DEFAULT ON RETURNS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-14, to amend the Companies Act (annual returns).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am going to take a rather unusual course on this bill so I want

to explain just how I came to get interested in it. In the last house, in following up some of the dealings of the former member for Port Arthur, I was checking up on a private holding company he happened to have because I was interested in discovering what relationship a certain very high civil servant had with this private company of the minister. I discovered that in the last year or two, though that company should have submitted a report to the Secretary of State (Mr. Courte-manche), no report had been submitted, and so I had to work on ancient information. Thus I submitted a question on the orders of the day to determine how many corporations were in default, in the years indicated, with regard to information summaries under section 125 of the Companies Act, and I discovered that there was a total in 1957 of 287 public companies and 893 private companies which were in default.
If any hon. members look up the penalty provided under that section they will find it is substantial. I wanted to know how many prosecutions had been laid against those companies in default and I was informed that there had never been any prosecutions. Fortunately I was never exposed to legal training, and this led me to ask the question: why have something in the law which provides a penalty which no one ever bothers to exercise? And so I felt the thing to do to clear up this situation of having 1,800 companies in default-in a sense, defying the law and yet the law not prosecuting them- was to abolish the whole matter, and so I went ahead with this amendment to the Companies Act. The first purpose of the amendment is to repeal subsection 4 of section 125 of the act. This is the section which says:
Where a company makes default in complying with any requirement of this section, it is liable to a fine not exceeding twenty dollars for every day during which the default continues, and every director and officer of the company who knowingly and willfully authorizes or permits the default is liable to the like penalty, and such fines may be recoverable on summary conviction.
After I had put the bill on the order paper I discovered through the Secretary of State -through the officials of that department -that they had already taken steps to clear up this very thing that I was after. Through the courtesy of the minister I was able to spend a considerable time examining the set-up of the Companies Act agency and just how the provisions of the act were carried out. It is a minor matter, and I am quite willing to concede it.
I am very pleased to hear that the Secretary of State was under way in his move to check up on this particular point before my bill was on the order paper, and because the
Companies Act
minister is now in the house and prepared to make a statement on the steps which have been taken I should like at this present time to yield the floor to the Secertary of State and have him make his statement with regard to this particular matter.
Hon. Henri Courtemanche (Secretary of
State): Mr. Speaker, the first purpose of this amendment is to repeal subsection 4 of section 125 of the Companies Act. This section applies to companies with share capital. The subsection to be repealed, at present reads as follows:
Where a company makes default in complying with any requirement of this section, it is liable to a fine not exceeding twenty dollars for every day during which the default continues, and every director and officer of the company who knowingly and willfully authorizes or permits the default is liable to the like penalty, and such fines may be recoverable on summary conviction.
The second purpose of the amendment is to ensure, by the proposed new subsection 4, that parliament is informed each year of any company which fails to file an annual summary in proper form with the Secretary of State. I think I should outline the reasons why the bill should not be enacted.
Even though no prosecutions were ever undertaken under subsection 4, nevertheless its very presence in the statute has a salutary effect. If circumstances arose where a company deliberately refused to file a return no effective means would be available to the department to enforce compliance by threat of prosecution or to have a penalty imposed by means of a prosecution if the subsection were repealed.
Furthermore, the presence of subsection 4 creates an offence for which an aggrieved party could launch a private prosecution, a right which would no longer be available if the subsection were repealed. There are approximately 12,000 companies which file the returns each year. These returns are required to be filed on or before June 1st in each year. In each year, there are approximately 1,500 companies which do not file by June 1 for a variety of reasons, such as the absence of a signing officer, oversight or a psychological abhorrence of business people to file government returns. The returns arrive in the department in a deluge from the middle of May to the middle of June each year and the departmental staff is busily engaged in processing the returns received. This processing takes approximately three months.
The primary purpose of the return is to have the information respecting the companies. Therefore, when the bulk of the returns received is disposed of, the department sends out a notice addressed to all companies

Companies Act
in default. There is no statutory requirement for this notice being mailed, but it is a practice taken to follow up on defaulting companies. This notice usually results in about 1,300 of the 1,500 defaulting companies filing the returns, leaving about 200 companies each year.
When these companies are in default to file returns for three consecutive years, subsection 9 of section 125 requires the Secretary of State to give notice, by registered letter addressed to the company or its president as shown by the last summary filed; that is, should the Secretary of State desire to apply to the company the sanction provided by subsections 9 and 10. By subsection 9 the company is required to prove to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State that it is still a subsisting company.
Under subsection 10 if, at the end of one month from the date of such notice the Secretary of State has not received a response from the company or its president, the company may be deemed not to be a subsisting corporation and no longer entitled to the sole use of its corporate name.
The registered notices mentioned in subsection 9 do not result in many of the defaulting companies submitting returns. These companies were incorporated by the applicants with high hopes which did not materialize, and they simply give up. The directors all resign, and there are no funds or assets in the company.
In a recent judgment of the court of appeal in the province of Quebec, in the Acme Vacuum case, it was held that even though a company does not file returns for three consecutive years and does not respond to the registered notice sent under subsection 9 the company does not lose its corporate status or the right to the sole use of its name, unless so deemed.
As a consequence of this decision the department now waits for 30 days for a reply to the notice. If no reply is received, a further 30 day period is allowed to elapse and then a further notice is sent to the company deeming it not to be a subsisting corporation.
The practice of sending this further notice was inaugurated in 1955, following the decision of the Quebec appeal court in the Acme Vacuum case reported in (1953) Queen's Bench 188, and 19 Canadian Practice Reports 45, and has not resulted in more than six companies establishing that they are subsisting and filing annual summaries in arrears.
I quite agree that in addition to the deterrent effect of subsection 4 it should be enforced where circumstances warrant a prosecution. Therefore, steps have been taken by the officers of the department to compile

a list of companies in default. A list of the companies -212 in number-in default to file summaries for the periods ending March 31, 1956 and 1957, together with a list of their directors, has been prepared. Notices are now being sent to these companies and their directors, together with arrival receipt cards pointing out the provisions of subsection (4). The reason that directors are being notified is to acquaint them with a knowledge of their obligations and because for a prosecution against a director to be successful he must have "knowingly and wilfully" authorized or permitted the default.
A further list of companies in default to file a summary for the period ending March 31, 1957 is also completed, together with the directors. This list contains the names of 350 companies. Notices are also being sent to these companies and their directors. Depending on the nature of the replies to be received investigation will be undertaken in co-operation with the officers of the department, the R.C.M.P. and the officers of the Department of Justice to ascertain the possibility of successful prosecutions. If the results of such investigation disclose that the companies are in fact carrying on business and that a prosecution would not prove abortive, such prosecutions will be undertaken.
I should also add that information is available in the department to any person who inquiries as to any specific company. The tariff of fees, as prescribed by P.C. 1954-1922 as amended by P.C. 1955-51 passed under section 141 of the Companies Act, contains an item-"Searches-each $1.00." There is another item entitled "Searches-within such categories as may be exempted by order of the Secretary of State-no fee". I can assure the house, through you, Mr. Speaker, that I am quite prepared to consider ordering that any inquiry by a member of parliament as to whether one or more specified companies have filed their annual summaries under section 125 in specified years be exempted under this item.
However, a list has not been prepared listing all companies in default to file annual summaries since confederation and those companies incorporated before 1867, which are subject to the Companies Act-although information is available with respect to each such company-because such would be a prodigious task at this late date.
Incidentally, if the bill were to be enacted it would necessitate other amendments to the Companies Act; for example, subsection (7) of section 125 would have to be repealed. Furthermore, as the proposed new subsection (4) would call for the names and addresses of

"managers" and "officers", subsection (1) paragraph (r) of section 125 would have to be amended to require disclosure of this information in the annual summary.
Representations have been received from members of the legal profession expressing the view that "the suggested report to parliament does not seem to have much merit, particularly if the penal clause is eliminated." It is also represented that the tabling in parliament of such lists would result in an unnecessary cluttering of parliament's records, bearing in mind that most companies actively carrying on their business do in fact file their returns and that the companies that are in default are largely inactive companies whose affairs would be of very little interest to more than a few people, and also that many companies use the non-filing of returns as a means of letting a company die and there is no improper intent in this, so far as the shareholders are concerned. I have already outlined the procedure following in the department under subsection (9) and (10) of section 125 with respect to defaulting companies, more particularly those that presumably are inactive and may be deemed to be no longer existing.
However, should there appear from this debate to be a general demand in the house for this, I would be glad to consider including a list of defaulting companies in the annual report of my department which is tabled in parliament. The report of the department for the year 1958-1959 for instance could list the companies which defaulted in 1958 and were still in default on March 31, 1959.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-15, to amend the Canada Elections Act (voting at advance polls).

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a strange bill to any hon. member who has been in the house in previous sessions or
Canada Elections Act
who is a veteran of this place. The last discussion on a bill similar in content to this took place on January 3, 1958. The subject matter of this bill is something that was a favourite of the former hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Knowles. The idea of it, of course, is very simple although the actual changes it entails are quite complex.
The purpose of the bill is to provide the opportunity to vote at an advance poll to any citizen of Canada who believes he is not going to be at his own poll on the ordinary polling day. The main reason for the development of advance poll provisions stems from the very great changes that have taken place in the social structure of our society. As many hon. members know, originally election day varied throughout Canada. It was not until the eighties that a consistent election day applicable throughout the country was established. We then had a long struggle to bring in advance poll provisions for people who would not be in their own constituencies on election day. Finally in 1920 provision was made for certain categories of workers including railway employees and fishermen.
Since 1920 there have been even more changes in our social setup. There has been a tremendous acceleration in the shift of population from rural to urban areas. People are engaged in travel to a greater extent and there are many more businessmen on the road. There is an increased tendency for people to plan vacations in advance, sometimes even months ahead. A general election can be called at any time because it is the prerogative of the Prime Minister to call a general election and frequently people are away at election time. There has been a vast increase in construction and bush work and various kinds of employment which takes people away from home. There is no adequate provision for the change that has occurred in our social organization.
The advance polls we have at the present time are set up to operate on the three days before the Sunday and Monday of the actual polling day. The intent of this bill is to set the advance polling date earlier which would involve moving back the nomination day from two to three weeks.
Perhaps that is one of the criticisms that could be made of the bill from, let us say, the point of view of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), because the Prime Minister's freedom of action in choosing the election date of course becomes circumscribed the more complicated the election act gets. If you move the nomination day farther back from the actual election day you limit the choice and the freedom of time in setting up the election.

Canada Elections Act
One of the other weaknesses of setting up advance polls is something we have to consider and that is the straight question of costs. A number of the provinces have gone into the provision of advance polls much more liberally than we have done in federal elections, and they have discovered that it is a fairly expensive business in terms of the number of votes that are actually cast. Any enthusiast of advance polls who looks at the election results in the Ontario general election of 1955 will quickly realize that the response to the advance poll provision was not as great as had been expected. No matter what provision you make it will be an infinitesimal part of the population which will vote at advance polls.
I am not deliberately trying to destroy the merit of this bill; I think the merit still exists. I am trying to anticipate the usual arguments.
When the former member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced his bill he made the point very clearly in relation to an election broadside that was put out by the first commoner of this house before the last general election. This broadside made the point that it was the Liberal government that was responsible for restricting the advance poll to such limited categories of people, and I think that argument is the one to keep to the fore, along with the fact that if the vote is a privilege that we have, every effort should be made to see that the privilege can be seized and taken advantage of.
I think that after the bill receives second reading it should be referred to the committee on privileges and elections and some sort of study should be made of how the provincial schemes are working and their costs before the bill is brought back from the committee for any further action.
There is little more that I wish to say. There is not much time left for any discussion of the bill, but I hope that members who do speak will stick to the point of whether the advance poll provision is a sound one from, let us say, the theoretical point of view and that we will not find them rambling off in the byways as we have had them do on certain other occasions when those private bills, especially those in connection with the elections act, and using this time as an opportunity for slanderous comment upon other parties who happen to have been involved in elections at various times.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second time within a week that I have followed the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in replying to a bill which he has proposed. I wish to assure him that this time I am going to agree

with him in principle. At the outset may I say I think it is quite clear that the present provisions for voting at advance polls are quite inadequate. I am definitely in favour of enlarging the provisions for voting at advance polls and I am in favour of the bill in principle, subject to one or two minor things which the hon. member himself has anticipated. Firstly, I think there should be no limit on the reason which must be advanced for a person to vote at an advance poll. At the present moment the person voting must have as a reason that he is going to be away on duty. That is a very disappointing reason to a good many people who go to advance polls in the hope of voting. If you want to find a reason you can always dream one up. In various instances, if the persons qualify to vote they do not have any trouble in finding the correct reason for doing so.
I also think there should be no limitation on the class of persons who are entitled to vote at an advance poll. When you try to limit the class of people you get into difficulties. One of the best examples I have heard of in recent times is that of a commercial traveller. At least he thought he was a commercial traveller until he went to vote. He was the purchasing agent for a large manufacturing company. He spends a good deal of his time on the road. He learned that commercial travellers were entitled to vote at advance polls, and so he presented himself to vote. When he presented himself there happened to be a rather sharp returning officer on hand who read to him the section about commercial travellers and it is set out in the explanatory note of the bill, and reads as follows:
'Commercial traveller' means a person employed on salary or on commission by a manufacturer or wholesale merchant to travel from place to place selling goods to or talcing orders for goods from, jobbers and retailers.
Of course, the act quite clearly states that he has to be selling goods, and this chap to whom I refer did not qualify as a commercial traveller and was not permitted to vote. This is the sort of thing you run into when you try to limit the number or the class of persons who may vote. Undoubtedly, when the act was first passed a commercial traveller was a person who went about the country selling for a wholesale establishment, but in the meantime the customs of the business world have changed to the point where there are now a good many people on the road who are commercial travellers and who try to do a selective job in purchasing for the company which they represent. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we should not try to limit the number or class of people who are to vote.

We have had many examples quoted in the house from time to time of people who ought to qualify and who are just slightly outside the strict group which has been laid down by the act. We all know of many people who have presented themselves at advance polls from time to time in the hope that they would be able to vote but because the act is so restrictive they found that they did not come within the proper class of people or that they were disqualified for some other reason such as not being away on duty.
I believe that the qualification to vote at advance polls should be as set out in this bill, namely substantially any person whose name appears on the list and who reasonably believes that he will not be present on election day. There is not much point in enlarging the class without opening up the act for all persons.
There is the other point the hon. member mentioned in connection with the time of holding an advance poll. Ten days before an election is a long time. Actually, a good many of the political parties and candidates set out at the beginning of an election to bring on a campaign. If they happen to be assisted by a high class advertising group, or by a person who is interested in and accustomed to selling goods and services or electoral candidates to the public, the campaign is started off on a slow basis and worked up to a climax a few days before election day.
A good many of the important and major speeches by party candidates, a good many of the ideas and matters that candidates want to bring forward, are left until a few days or a week before the actual voting day. A person who wants to vote at an advance poll has not received the benefit, if it can be called such, of campaign literature which he might otherwise have benefited from. Mind you, he may not even appreciate it. He may be the type of voter who would much prefer to make up his own mind a month before he votes, but regardless of that he has not been made acquainted with all the issues that the candidates wish to place before him.
I feel that ten days prior to voting day is quite a long time before voting day for advance polls and that the person who would vote at such an advance poll would not vote with the same knowledge and facts in his mind as a person who would go to the polls ten days later. That is one difficulty. I believe I understand the reason for the ten day period. In the first place, if we are going to open up the provision with respect to voting at advance polls to every person who is going to be away for any good and valid reason we are going to have a larger number of people
57071-3-78|
Canada Elections Act
voting at advance polls and if such polls are held on the Thursday, Friday and Saturday before election day as is the case now I can foresee that it will be practically impossible for returning officers to get proper lists of those who have already voted to the different polls.
These difficulties are certainly great. I have no doubt that even under the present system there is difficulty in that some person who wants to vote twice and thus break the regulations of the elections act can still do so. I perceive that there are two different situations so far as urban and rural polls are concerned. In the case of urban polls the difficulty under present conditions is the lack of ability to identify voters. On the other hand, it is safe to say that in a small rural poll of 50 to 150 people the deputy returning officer will know every person who presents himself to vote or if he does not the poll clerk or one of the scrutineers will. This is certainly not true in the case of the larger urban polls where no one may be aware of the actual identity of the person and it is very easy for a person to misrepresent himself.
But I do not think this difficulty is sufficient to justify advancing the date for advance polls. A person can now come along with identification, not be the person he claims to be and vote, thus contravening the elections act.
There is another difficulty in the case of rural polls. There the difficulty does not concern identification but the distribution of lists of persons who have already voted. In the case of rural polls there are great distances to be covered. With respect to urban polls, it is a very simple matter geographically for the returning officer to distribute lists of persons who have voted by going from one place to another in a reasonably short space of time. It is next to impossible to do so in the case of the larger rural polls where the polling subdivisions are often many hundreds of miles apart.
In the result, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the principle of the bill that we should enlarge the provisions for voting. We should enlarge the group who are entitled to vote at advance polls. I would be inclined to leave the time of voting as it is now. Let it be proved by trial and error whether it is satisfactory.
I think it has been found that there are not too many who actually vote at advance polls. Granted that the number will increase when more are entitled, nevertheless I would not anticipate the terrific influx of people wanting to vote at advance polls that might be expected by some. If the act is to be amended I think it would be sufficient for the moment at least to enlarge the eligible group and leave the time of voting as it now exists.
